title: Marcus doesn't want to get up
hookLine: the emperor argues with himself under the blankets: was I made to lie here warm?
carry: up, to do a human's work

lines: A COLD TENT BY THE DANUBE.
cards: A cold tent, maybe somewhere near the Danube, in the second century. It's early. The most powerful man in the world is lying under his blankets, and he does not want to get up.
He's Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome. And instead of getting up, or staying put, he does something odd. He argues with himself about it, in writing.

teach.b: Welcome to camp two, the stories: from today, the words become people. Marcus was a Stoic.
The Stoics were philosophers of ancient Greece and Rome who taught that a good life is built from what you do with what happens to you.
He kept a private notebook, the one from camp one, and much of it was probably written on military campaigns in his last decade.

teach.h: BOOK FIVE STARTS UNDER THE BLANKETS.
teach.b: Book five opens right there, under the blankets. In George Long's translation, he tells himself that when he rises unwillingly, he should remember: "I am rising to the work of a human being."

Then he asks: "Or have I been made for this, to lie in the bed-clothes and keep myself warm?" And he answers himself back: but it's more pleasant here. The emperor of Rome, haggling with his own pillow.

teach.h: THE ANTS, THE SPIDERS, THE BEES.
teach.b: The little plants, the birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees, all busy doing their part to keep the world in order. And you, a human being, won't do yours? It's easy to hear that as a scolding.
But notice what he doesn't say.
Not get up to be rich, or well-known, or because the empire needs you. Get up because there's a human's work to do, and you're a human.

teach.h: THE WORK OF A HUMAN BEING.
teach.b: Being kind, being fair, being useful to the people around you: for a Stoic, that was the job description. The alarm isn't a punishment. It's a reminder of what you're for.
And this isn't a sage who never struggled. It's a tired man winning a very small argument, one morning at a time, and writing it down so he'd remember.

how: Many people who practice Stoicism today begin the morning with a short reflection, often reading Marcus Aurelius, and remind themselves of the day's duties and the kind of person they want to be in them.

o: a Roman emperor who argued with himself in a private notebook
a Roman general who wrote a well-known history of his wars
a Greek poet who wrote hymns to the gods of Olympus

games.q: the emperor and his blankets — tap the pairs.
p: a life built from what you do

Marcus argues back at himself that staying in bed is more pleasant
the emperor of Rome, haggling with his own pillow.

games.q: you're the emperor of Rome. it's cold, it's early, and you don't want to get up. what do you do?
o: stay in bed. you're the emperor.
argue with yourself in writing, then get up.
order someone else to do today's work.
games.why: he argues it out on the page: was I made to lie here warm? then he points at the ants and the bees, and reminds himself of a human's work.

practice: From today, the bell gives you two minutes: sit, and let the breath settle. Picture tomorrow's alarm and the pull of the warm covers, then picture yourself getting up at the first alarm, just once, feet on the floor.
Ask Marcus's question, what's the human's work waiting for me today, and let one answer come: a person to be kind to, or a job to do well.

wordCard.voice: Marcus Aurelius. An emperor arguing with his own blankets, and reminding himself what a human being is for.

orig.note: Greek: to himself, the title the Meditations carry in the manuscripts. A Roman emperor wrote his private notebook in Greek.

carryVoice: Your line: up, to do a human's work. An emperor needed reminding every morning, too. Day twenty-two, done.
